A two-lesson visual course · Peoples of the Volga

The Mari People: Who They Are, and How They Have Been Seen

Origins, language, faith, numbers and survival of the people once called “Cheremis”, with maps, charts and a fact-check

Prepared by Scholar · 15 November 2026

The Mari are a Finno-Ugric people of the middle Volga in Russia. Their own name for themselves, mari, means “person”. Russians called them Cheremis for centuries. About 424,000 live in Russia, and more than half of them in the Republic of Mari El. This course has two lessons. Lesson 1 explains who they are: language family, early history, groups, where they live and how many they are. Lesson 2 covers faith, culture and survival: the native religion, dress and music, the Soviet years, the 1990s revival, language policy, how ethnic Russians have seen the Mari, and a fact-check on a claim of an “armed movement”.

The course began from a short summary text. Every figure in it was checked, and where research corrected the text this is stated in the box “What the research changed”. Sources in Russian and other local languages come first, then English; each claim carries a link and a date. Tags: confirmed (a primary record or two independent sources), disputed (sources disagree), unsupported (no evidence found), estimate (a modeled figure or my own arithmetic). Items I could not check in a second source carry [unconfirmed]. In the section on how Russians see the Mari, “confirmed” means only that the named source says it, never that a stereotype is true. Jargon is explained where it first appears and again in the glossary.

The short answer

  • Who they are. A Uralic-language people who took shape between the Volga and the Vyatka in the first millennium AD. Of 423,803 Mari in Russia in 2021, 246,560 live in Mari El. confirmed
  • Language relatives. Mari is not “related to Mordvin” in any close sense. The “Volgaic” pairing is rejected; Mari shares far more with Komi and Udmurt (Permic). confirmed
  • Decline. The number of Mari fell about 34% from the 1989 peak (643,698) to 2021. The reasons are not measured in the sources I read. confirmed [unconfirmed]
  • Mari El. The often-quoted 40% Mari and 52.5% Russians are shares of residents who stated a nationality. Of all residents, Mari are 36.4% and Russians 47.7%. confirmed
  • Religion. Most religious Mari are Orthodox; many mix it with the native religion. No measured share follows the native religion; “20–25%” has no source. disputed
  • Politics. The 2005 European Parliament resolution is about human rights, press freedom, the 2004 election and language education. It does not name Markelov or say “Russification”. Separatism was a fringe in 1990–95. confirmed
  • How Russians have seen the Mari. The image moved from warriors to pagans to “wild” peasants of a lower rank, and, in some modern speech and media, to sorcerers. Surveys show Mari reporting insults more often than Russians do. Jokes and identity hiding are not studied in the sources I found. confirmed [unconfirmed]
  • The “armed Mari movement trained in Finnish camps”. No evidence found. The story traces to a 2005 wave of press articles after a political speech about oil and foreign pressure. unsupported

1Lesson one

Who the Mari are

Sections 1–7 · name, language family, early history, groups, distribution, numbers, language today

1. A name, and what it means

The Mari call themselves mari (also written marij or mary). In Mari the word means “person”, “man” or “husband” [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018] confirmed. Radio Svoboda adds that scholars of language and history say the Mari used this word for their identity and did not accept the outsiders’ name “Cheremis” [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018].

For centuries Russians called the Mari Cheremis (Russian cheremisy). The word is an exonym: a name given to a people by outsiders. Its origin is uncertain disputed. Radio Svoboda says linguists think it has Uralic roots but that there is no final version; the readings it lists are “a man of the tribe chere (char, sar)” and “a warlike forest man” [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018]. Another view in the wider literature, that it is a Turkic name given by neighbors, I did not check [unconfirmed].

The name is old. According to Radio Svoboda, a letter attributed to the Khazar ruler Joseph (961) lists a people called cármis among those paying him tribute, and the Russian Primary Chronicle lists the Cheremis among peoples paying tribute to Rus [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018]. I read this only in the news article, not in the sources themselves, and the date of the chronicle’s list is uncertain [unconfirmed].

The Mari disliked the exonym. A congress of the Mari people held in Kazan on 12–24 February 1918 decided to drop “Cheremis”, because it was not a name of their own, and to use “Mari” instead [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018] confirmed. Radio Svoboda says that Russians and other neighbors first kept the old name, then slowly adopted the new one, and that in Soviet times “Cheremis” was felt to be offensive [Radio Svoboda, 29 Jan 2018]. In Lesson 2 we return to the word, because it later became a mild insult in everyday speech.

Why it matters

A name is a first sign of who has the power to describe whom. “Mari” is the people’s own word. “Cheremis” is what others called them. Tracing the change shows how the Mari came to speak for themselves in public life.

2. A language family, and a correction

Mari is a Uralic language. The Uralic family includes Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, Komi, Udmurt, Saami, Nenets and several others. The older term Finno-Ugric names the large branch that holds everything except the Samoyedic languages (Nenets and its relatives). Many linguists now doubt that this branch is a true unit with a single common ancestor, so treat it as a convenient label disputed [Blažek, 2012] [Häkkinen, 2012]. A protolanguage is the reconstructed common ancestor of a group of related languages.

A starting text for this course said the Mari are “related to Mordvins”. That needs care. The Mari and the Mordvins (Erzya and Moksha) are neighbors on the Volga, and for a long time books grouped them as a “Volgaic” branch. Václav Blažek (2012) argues that this branch does not hold. He counts shared word-and-sound features (called isoglosses): about 150 link Mari with the Permic languages (Komi and Udmurt), about 110 link Mordvin with the Finnic languages, and only about 20 link Mordvin with Mari. He adds that another scholar, Salminen (2002), accepts “Volgaic” at most as a geographic grouping [Blažek, 2012] confirmed. Jaakko Häkkinen proposes a different first split, between an eastern and a western-central group, and says deeper branches remain unsettled [Häkkinen, 2012] disputed.

Verdict. Mari and Mordvin are both Uralic and are neighbors, but “Mari is related to Mordvin” as a close genetic pair is not the current view. Mari is closest to Permic in the studies cited.

Why it matters

The Uralic link explains why Estonia, Finland and Hungary take a cultural interest in the Mari. It does not mean the Mari are “the same people” as Finns or Hungarians. Languages can be related while the peoples’ histories and daily lives differ widely.

3. Origins and early history

Scholars summarized in the Ethnoencyclopedia hold that the Mari took shape in the first millennium AD between the Volga and Vyatka rivers, from Finno-Ugric tribes whose ancestors belonged to the Ananyino, Gorodets and Azelino archaeological cultures [Etnosy, 2026] confirmed. An archaeological culture is a set of sites that share tools, pottery and building styles.

In the Middle Ages the Mari lived between larger powers: Volga Bulgaria, then the Golden Horde, then the Kazan Khanate, a Tatar state whose capital was Kazan. Dates for the khanate’s start differ between sources (the 1430s or 1440s; 1438 and 1445 are both given) disputed. It ended when Ivan IV (“the Terrible”) took Kazan in October 1552.

The Mari were not one political body. In the account attributed to Prince Andrei Kurbsky, a Russian nobleman who defected to Poland, the Hill Mari on the right bank of the Volga joined the Muscovites early in the campaign, while the more numerous Meadow Mari on the left bank stayed hostile to the “Christian army” [Luehrmann, 2013]. The same chronicler calls the Cheremis a “large and very bloodthirsty” tribe, which the scholar Luehrmann reads as a sign that sixteenth-century sources noticed their fighting skill rather than any magic [Luehrmann, 2013]. Treat these as the views of a Russian-side writer, not as a neutral record.

The official history on the Russian foreign ministry’s Mari El page tells it this way: Hill Mari envoys asked Ivan IV for protection in late 1546; the right-bank lands joined Russia in June 1551; and the Meadow Mari swore an oath to the tsar on 10 October 1552 after Kazan fell [Russian MFA, 2026]. This is an official narrative that presents accession as voluntary, so I tag it disputed. Russians built the fort of Sviyazhsk in 1551 [Orthodox Encyclopedia, 2026] confirmed, and later the forts of Kozmodemyansk (1583) and Tsarevokokshaysk (1584), which became Yoshkar-Ola [Orthodox Encyclopedia, 2026] [City of Yoshkar-Ola, 2026] confirmed.

Fighting went on for about three decades. The Cheremis wars are usually dated 1552–1557, 1571/72–1574 and 1581–1584, but sources shift the years by one or two disputed [Finno-Ugric Centre, 2026] [Tatarica, 2026]. They were not only a defense of the old religion. They also grew out of taxes, army service during the Livonian War, and the Crimean raids of the same years [Finno-Ugric Centre, 2026] [Tatarica, 2026]. Mari, Tatars, Chuvash, Udmurts and Mordvins all took part, according to the Tatarica entry.

Key dates
  1. 1st millennium ADMari take shape between the Volga and the Vyatka
  2. 1551Russians build Sviyazhsk; Hill Mari join Russia
  3. Oct 1552Kazan falls to Ivan IV
  4. 1552–1584Three “Cheremis wars”
  5. Feb 1918Congress replaces “Cheremis” with “Mari”
  6. 4 Nov 1920Mari Autonomous Oblast created
  7. 1989Peak: 643,698 Mari in Russia
  8. 2021Census: 423,803
Why it matters

The conquest of Kazan split the Mari between those who sided with Moscow and those who fought it. Both memories still shape how Mari speak about their past today, from state ceremonies to the “Cheremis” song discussed in Lesson 2.

4. Three groups, two written languages

Mari scholars and the census describe three main groups. Meadow Mari (also called Lugovo-Mari) live mostly on the left bank of the Volga and are the more numerous group [Luehrmann, 2013] [Rosstat 2021, table 4, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)]. Hill Mari (gornye mariytsy) live on the hilly right bank. Eastern Mari live farther east, in Bashkortostan and the Urals; the census shows large Mari communities there today [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)]. The Rantanen language database also marks a small North-Western Mari area [Rantanen et al., 2022]. Rosstat counts Meadow and Eastern Mari together as “Meadow-Eastern Mari” and lists Hill Mari separately [Rosstat 2021, table 4, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. When and why the eastern groups moved is not covered in the sources I opened [unconfirmed].

The two largest groups have separate literary standards, that is, agreed written forms used in schools, books and newspapers. The Meadow-Eastern and Hill standards took shape in the 1920s, and a linguistic article from 1995 discusses whether they could be merged [Ivanov, 1995] confirmed. A St. Petersburg book of 1775 titled Compositions belonging to the grammar of the Cheremis language is described as the first Mari grammar, and the title page shows its date and place of printing confirmed. I did not verify the claim that it was the first [unconfirmed].

In the 2021 census, 14,077 people in Russia named themselves Hill Mari, and 13,953 of them lived in Mari El; a further 101 gave “Meadow-Eastern Mari” as a nationality [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. Some Hill Mari may have answered simply “Mari”, so the Hill count may be too low.

Why it matters

Counting Mari as one people hides real differences of dialect and history. The two literary standards mean that teaching and publishing in Mari often needs two parallel sets of books.

5. Where the Mari live

The Republic of Mari El lies on the left bank of the middle Volga, north of the Chuvash Republic and west of Tatarstan. Its capital is Yoshkar-Ola. In 2021, 246,560 of the 423,803 Mari in Russia (58%) lived in the republic. The other 42% live in the Volga–Ural region and beyond: Bashkortostan has 84,988, Kirov Oblast 18,766, Tatarstan 15,666 and Sverdlovsk Oblast 13,995 [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. In 1989 about half lived in the republic (324,349 of 643,698), by our own arithmetic from Demoscope’s tables [Demoscope, 2026] [Demoscope, 2026].

Mari El is mainly rural. In 2021, 138,831 of its Mari lived in villages and 107,729 in towns (44% urban) [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. In 2005 the Helsinki Federation report found that Mari were only about a quarter of Yoshkar-Ola’s people but about 70% of the rural population [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006]; that is older data and should not be read as today’s figure.

6. How many Mari are there?

The 2021 census counted 423,803 Mari in Russia [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. Figure 11 shows the series since 1897. The count rose to a peak of 643,698 in 1989 and then fell at every census: by 39,400 to 2002, by a further 56,693 to 2010, and by 123,802 to 2021. Over the whole period from 1989 the drop is about 34% [Demoscope, 2026] [Demoscope, 2026] [Kidsher, 2023] [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)]. The sources I read report the fall but do not measure its causes. Possible factors that scholars and Mari commentators discuss are a change in the nationality people declare, an aging population, migration, and low birth rates, but I could not confirm their weights [unconfirmed].

Now look at Mari El itself. The 40% and 52.5% that are often quoted are shares of those who stated a nationality. In 2021, 677,097 people lived in the republic and 614,959 gave a nationality. Russians were 322,932 (52.5% of those stating, 47.7% of all residents), Mari 246,560 (40.1% of those stating, 36.4% of all residents), Tatars 29,317 (4.8%) and Chuvash 3,656 (0.6%) [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. The number of Mari in the republic grew to 324,349 in 1989 (43.3% of the population), then fell to 246,560 [Demoscope, 2026] [Demoscope, 2026] [Rosstat 2021, table 1, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)].

Why it matters

Who counts as “the titular people” matters in politics. A titular republic is a republic named after one nationality; in Mari El the Mari are the named nation but a minority of residents. Russians outnumber Mari there, and the gap is widening.

7. The language today

Mari and Russian are both state languages of Mari El, under the republic’s 1995 constitution and its language law, which treat Meadow and Hill Mari as official forms [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed. The word endangered is often used for Mari by activists and some linguists. I did not check UNESCO’s Atlas of endangered languages, so its exact rating is not confirmed [unconfirmed].

The 2021 census asked people which languages they speak. Across Russia, 258,722 said they can speak Meadow-Eastern Mari, 15,352 Hill Mari and 229 gave a third label, together 274,303. Of these, about 89% said they use it in daily life [Rosstat 2021, table 4, 2022 (archived 6 Aug 2023)] confirmed. In Mari El the total was 164,450, and in Bashkortostan 62,135. These are self-reported answers: they show what people say, not how well or how often they speak.

Earlier counts were higher. Compiled tables give about 451,000 speakers of Meadow Mari and 36,800 of Hill Mari in 2002, and about 365,000 and 23,100 in 2010 [unconfirmed]. If the series is right, the number of speakers fell by roughly 40% in two decades. I did not open the Rosstat tables for 2002 and 2010, and one Mari news site printed the 2002 number as a 2010 number, so treat these two years with caution.

A study quoted by the Helsinki Federation found that 96% of Mari in Russia named Mari as their native language in 1959 and 82% in 1989 (urban Mari: 77% and 70%). A survey in 2005 found that only about half of Mari in Mari El used the language regularly at home [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed. Earlier, in 2001, the Mari Research Institute found that 70.1% of Mari said they speak Mari with their parents [Regnum / Mari Research Institute, 12 Aug 2002]. The questions differ, so the numbers do not contradict each other.

Why it matters

A language can fall quickly in one generation if parents stop speaking it to children. The 2021 numbers, together with the school data in Lesson 2, show a language that most Mari still speak but that fewer young people use.

Review questions, lesson 1

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What does the self-name “mari” mean, and why did a 1918 congress drop the name “Cheremis”?
Answer. “Mari” means “person” or “man”. “Cheremis” was a name given by outsiders, of uncertain origin, and the delegates felt it was not a national name. They decided on 12–24 February 1918 in Kazan to use “Mari”.
2A source says the Mari are “related to Mordvins”. What is the more accurate statement?
Answer. Both are Uralic languages and neighbors on the Volga. The old “Volgaic” grouping of Mari and Mordvin is now rejected. In the studies cited, Mari shares many more features with Permic (Komi and Udmurt) than with Mordvin.
3Name the three main Mari groups and the two literary standards.
Answer. Meadow, Hill and Eastern Mari. The standards are Meadow-Eastern and Hill, formed in the 1920s.
4In Mari El in 2021 the Mari were “40%” and Russians “52.5%”. Of what are these shares?
Answer. Of the 614,959 residents who stated a nationality. Of all 677,097 residents, Mari were 36.4% and Russians 47.7%.
5By how much did the number of Mari in Russia fall from 1989 to 2021, and what do the sources say about the cause?
Answer. From 643,698 to 423,803, about 34%. The sources report the fall but do not measure its causes.
6Why is it hard to say how many Mari speak the language, and what does the 2021 census show?
Answer. The census records only what people say. In 2021, about 274,000 people in Russia said they speak a Mari language, and about 89% of them said they use it in daily life. The 2002 and 2010 speaker figures are from compiled tables that were not checked.

2Lesson two

Faith, culture and survival

Sections 1–8 · religion, baptism, craft, Soviet years, politics, how Russians have seen the Mari, language policy, fact-check

1. The native religion

Most religious Mari are Orthodox Christians. The Etnosy encyclopedia says that mass baptism of the Mari took place in the 18th and 19th centuries, that many follow a “Mari faith” that mixes Christianity with the older religion, and that the older religion is stronger among the Eastern Mari [Etnosy, 2026] confirmed. Practitioners of the older religion call it by several names. Scholars argue about what to call it: “paganism”, “ethnic religion”, even “shamanism” [Manuscript, 2020] [Christensen, 2017] disputed. This course uses “native religion”.

The religion centers on sacred groves, stands of trees where people gather to pray and make offerings. A kart is a priest who leads the prayers. The leading deity is called Kugu Yumo (“Great God”); NG-Religii writes Osh Kugu Yumo. In 1837 the exiled writer Alexander Herzen described what he saw in Vyatka province: the Mari held a supreme spirit, “Yuma”, whose power was shared with his consort “Yuman-ava” and with other gods; the priests (karts) were chosen “from the cleverest and most experienced Cheremis” and interpreted dreams and made predictions; services were held in “clean, sacred places” belonging to one family or a whole village [Herzen, via Aiplatov, 2012]. This is an outsider’s report from the 1830s, not a modern believer’s description.

How many groves are there? NG-Religii wrote in 2010 that there are “about 520” [NG-Religii, 20 Oct 2010]. A report in Potok Media on the registration of groves gives 327 [Potok Media, 2026]. I could not tell whether the two counts measure the same thing (all groves, or only registered ones) disputed [unconfirmed].

Official policy has changed several times. According to NG-Religii, the Mari ASSR’s environmental law of 17 April 1991 put “religious-cultural zones” under protection and banned felling in places of traditional Mari prayer; the first republic president, Vladislav Zotin, was blessed at his inauguration in December 1991 by both an Orthodox bishop and the head pagan priest; and the group Oshmari-Chimari (“White Mari – Pure Mari”) was registered on 6 June 1991. The same article says that President Markelov repealed the 1991 law by a decree of 13 March 2001, and that in February 2008 the felling of 71 birches in a grove near the village of Tapsher caused a public outcry, after which the authorities promised to protect the groves [NG-Religii, 20 Oct 2010] confirmed.

How many people follow the native religion?

Nobody knows. The census does not help: the question list of the 2020 census, set by Rosstat order no. 553, contains no question on religion [Rosstat programme, 17 Sep 2020] confirmed. All numbers below come from other sources and measure different things.

FigureWhat it measuresSourceStatus
67.3% Orthodox, 14% “pagans” (chimari), 5% MuslimsOfficial figures for residents of Mari El, given by the republic’s culture minister about 2007 (NG-Religii, 2010, says “three years ago”); method not given[NG-Religii, 20 Oct 2010]confirmed that it was said; estimate
15.4% of MariShare who said the native religion is a uniting factor of Mari identity (not the share who practice it)[Glukhova & Glukhov, 2003]confirmed
About 6% of adults (about 15% of Mari)A figure from a 2012 atlas of religion in Russia, seen only secondhand in search resultssource not opened[unconfirmed]
25–50% of MariAn estimate attributed to the ethnologist Viktor Shnirelman, seen only secondhandsource not opened[unconfirmed]

A starting text for this course gave “20–25%”. I could not find a measured figure that matches it; the numbers I found fall anywhere from a few percent to half of all Mari, depending on who counts and how disputed.

Why it matters

When you read a percentage for “followers” of a religion, ask who was counted and how. A person can attend church, take part in a grove ceremony, and answer “Orthodox” on a form, all in the same year.

2. Baptism, dual faith and a 19th-century movement

Baptism of non-Russians in the Volga region was a state policy. The Office of New Converts, created by a decree of the Holy Synod of 23 August 1731, ran its largest campaign after an imperial decree of 11 September 1740. Over 1741–64 it is credited with baptizing more than 400,000 non-Orthodox subjects of the empire. It was closed by a Senate decree of 6 April 1764 [Tatarica, 2026] confirmed. The Tatarica entry does not give a separate count for the Mari.

Baptism did not end the old practice. NG-Religii describes dual faith (Russian dvoeverie), meaning that people are formally baptized and go to church but hold their life-cycle rites in the groves, and do not distinguish between the “Russian” God and Kugu Yumo, worshipping both as one Creator. The article quotes Orthodox clergy who say that in some villages dual-faith believers still bring sacrificial geese to the church and leave them under the icon of St. George [NG-Religii, 20 Oct 2010] confirmed. Luehrmann adds that periodic revivals of Mari ritual took place throughout the 19th century in officially Christian villages, and drew strong attention from missionaries [Luehrmann, 2013].

One revival grew into a distinct movement. Kugu Sorta (“Great Candle”) took shape in the 1870s in the Yaransk district of Vyatka province. Its members called themselves “white Mari” (osh mari). The founders changed the old pantheon, rites and ethics, and the members were repeatedly harassed by local church and civil authorities. Pesetskaya reports about 200 members in the 1890s (citing Popov), an official count of 273 in 1912, and an unofficial observation from the same period that almost half of the Cheremis population of three neighboring districts “leaned toward” it [Pesetskaya, 2018] confirmed disputed. The official and unofficial counts disagree, so the real size is unclear.

Why it matters

The “Mari faith” was never a single church. Villages, families and eras differed, and the state, the Orthodox church and the Mari themselves all shaped what it became.

3. Dress, music and craft

Mari embroidery is known for geometric patterns in red on white linen. The museum record of the Estonian National Museum describes the shirt below as a Mari woman’s shirt (around 1900); the same museum holds the sash shown next to it confirmed. I did not find a scholarly source in this research that explains the symbolism of particular patterns, so I make no claims about it [unconfirmed].

Music appears in the 19th-century ethnographic literature. Gustav-Theodor Pauli’s Ethnographic Description of the Peoples of Russia (1862) writes that at weddings “the sounds of drums and of instruments reminiscent of a bagpipe” call the villagers to a meadow, where the young men dance noisily on the grass while the girls shyly watch [Pauli, 1862] confirmed.

4. The Soviet period and the 1990s

After the revolution, the Mari first gained their own territory. The Mari Autonomous Oblast was created on 4 November 1920 and became an autonomous republic (ASSR) on 5 December 1936. On 22 October 1990 it became the Mari Soviet Socialist Republic, a step the Helsinki report ties to the sovereignty declaration of that October, part of the “parade of sovereignties” across the USSR. On 17 April 1991 it became the “Mari SSR – Republic of Mari El” and on 8 July 1992 simply the “Republic of Mari El – Mari El”; its third constitution was adopted on 24 June 1995 [State Assembly of Mari El, 2026] [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed. One US historian gives October rather than November 1920 for the oblast [Retish, 2002] disputed. Yoshkar-Ola took its present name in 1928; its older names were Tsarevokokshaysk and, from 1919, Krasnokokshaysk [City of Yoshkar-Ola, 2026] confirmed.

The Mari national movement began in 1917, when a Mari Union (Mari Ushem) and an All-Russia Congress of the Mari were organized. It split into a liberal and a radical wing, and by late 1918 the radical wing had taken control of what remained [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed. In the 1930s, according to the Helsinki report, many Mari writers, teachers and scholars were killed or imprisoned; the report says an estimate of “as many as 2,000” Mari intellectuals killed exists, but that the full effects have not been documented [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] estimate [unconfirmed]. A Mari scholar describes one case: in early 1937, Aidush Elchibaev, director of the Mari state pedagogical institute, told an open party meeting that the institute should recruit more national cadres, and “that was enough” to put him on the list of “bourgeois nationalists”; he was arrested in 1937 [Oshaev, 2022] confirmed. Educational reforms of the late 1950s ended compulsory study of the titular languages across the USSR, and the Helsinki report says Russian grew steadily more dominant [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed.

Perestroika brought a revival. In April 1990 Mari Ushem was reborn “after 70 years” and helped draft the sovereignty declaration. In late 1990 a radical minority split off as Kugeze Mlande (“Ancestral Land”), which, among other things, called for independence for Mari El; it stayed a fringe movement and was reportedly dissolved in 1995 [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] confirmed. The mainstream movement’s declared aims were cultural and civic.

5. The Markelov era and the European Parliament

Leonid Markelov was president (later titled head) of Mari El from 2001 until April 2017, when he left office [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] [Kommersant, 7 Apr 2017] confirmed. The International Helsinki Federation and the Moscow Helsinki Group report that the 2004 election was unfair, with administrative pressure on public employees, and list attacks on critical journalists, including Yelena Rogacheva of Radio Free Europe (January 2005) and Vladimir Kozlov, editor of the Finno-Ugric newspaper Kudo+Kodu and head of the Mari national movement’s council (February 2005) [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006]. These are the findings of the report’s authors, a human-rights group. The authorities’ side is not in that document [unconfirmed]. In February 2005 Russian federal newspapers framed the Kozlov case differently: Rossiyskaya Gazeta wrote that the beating was “politicized” and that a “nationalist label” produced a scandal in the West, as reported by Parkkonen [Parkkonen, Oct 2005].

On 12 May 2005 the European Parliament passed a resolution on Mari El. A starting text said it criticized “Markelov-era Russification”. The text of the resolution (P6_TA(2005)0185) is about human rights, press freedom, the 2004 election and equal treatment of Mari in language education. It does not name Markelov, and I found the word “Russification” nowhere in it [European Parliament, 12 May 2005] confirmed. If you read that the resolution “condemned Russification”, that is a paraphrase by someone else.

Markelov’s successor, Alexander Yevstifeyev, was elected in September 2017, as TASS reported [TASS, Sep 2017] confirmed.

6. How ethnic Russians have seen the Mari

How to read this section. It reports what writers, officials and surveys said about the Mari at different times. A reported stereotype is not a fact about the Mari. “Confirmed” here means only that the named source says it. The same tags are used as elsewhere in the course.
What is missing. I found no systematic study of jokes about the Mari, no representative survey on Mari hiding their identity, no Mari-specific item in the Levada reports I read, and no usable Mari-language source to quote. Each is marked below as unconfirmed.

6.1 Warriors first, “pagans” next (16th–18th centuries)

Sonja Luehrmann, a historian and anthropologist who studies Mari society, argues that early Russian sources did not call the Cheremis sorcerers. They described fighters. Prince Kurbsky called them a “large and very bloodthirsty” tribe, and the Austrian envoy Herberstein wrote that men and women alike were fast runners and skilled archers, sought after as foot soldiers by both Moscow and Kazan [Luehrmann, 2013]. After Russian rule firmed up, she says, the image changed. In the 1630s the German diplomat Adam Olearius wrote that “all those who live around Kazan are pagans, for they are neither circumcised nor baptized”; the Cheremis man he met answered a question about who made heaven and earth with “The devil knows”; and the Cheremis on his ship, he says, were afraid of it and some ran away [Luehrmann, 2013]. Luehrmann’s reading is that “unusual and irrational beliefs have replaced military might as the defining features of the Maris” [Luehrmann, 2013]. That is her interpretation of these travelers, not a view she says all Russians held.

Later travelers repeated the theme. Luehrmann notes that the 18th-century scholars Johann Georgi and Gerhard Müller described the Cheremis and Chuvash in terms of their “pagan” gods and customs, which, they wrote, were kept up even after baptism [Luehrmann, 2013].

6.2 The 19th century: “wild”, “brown mice”, and a ranking of peoples

In 1837, while exiled to Vyatka, Herzen wrote a short ethnographic note, printed in January 1838. The Mari historian Gennady Aiplatov reads it as an attempt to draw attention and sympathy to the peoples oppressed by tsarism [Herzen, via Aiplatov, 2012]. Of the Mari it says: “The temper of the Cheremis differs from that of the Votyaks [Udmurts] in that they lack their shyness. On the contrary, there is something wild, stubborn in them” («в них есть что-то дикое, упорное») [Herzen, via Aiplatov, 2012] confirmed. In a memoir of his 1835 journey to Vyatka, quoted by Aiplatov, he wrote that the “poor, wretched tribes of Cheremis, Votyaks, Chuvash and Zyrians” filled him with melancholy [Herzen, via Aiplatov, 2012]. The historian Aaron Retish reads such texts as part of a hierarchy: ethnographers in Vyatka ranked Tatars above Mari and Udmurts below, and Herzen put Russians first, Mari as “maturing” and Udmurts as “primitive savages” [Retish, 2002]. Retish adds that many state officials described Udmurts and Mari as “brown mice” and “filthy people”, and that a Vyatka governor said Udmurts “do not have the ability to do factory work” [Retish, 2002].

Pauli’s 1862 entry on the Mari, in a book published for the empire’s millennium, strikes a milder note and a different one: “The Cheremis love feasts… at which they drink beer without measure”, especially at weddings and harvest festivals that last several weeks [Pauli, 1862] confirmed. Such lines show how even a friendly ethnographer fixed a single habit, here drinking, on a whole people.

The Russian historian Nikita Pislegin found similar language in official papers. A statistical description of Vyatka province of 1850 and surveys of the 1850s and early 1860s said that Mari were “wild” (дики), while Bashkirs and Teptyars were “rude, insolent, cruel, lazy, treacherous and poor” and Tatars “prone to lawsuits, theft, fraud” [Pislegin, 2023] confirmed. He also notes how the word “Cheremis” itself could be used as an insult: in 1846 the mayor of Sarapul called a town councillor a “cheremisin”, and Pislegin sees both an ethnic and a religious meaning there, the identification of the insulted man with a non-Christian [Pislegin, 2023] confirmed. Retish’s footnote says the old names for Mari (“Cheremis”) and Udmurts (“Votyak”) now carry a pejorative sense [Retish, 2002] confirmed.

6.3 The word “inorodtsy”

Inorodtsy (singular inorodets) was a legal and everyday word of imperial Russia for non-Russian subjects, literally “people of another birth”. A 2014 article in a Russian journal traces it: the adjective first meant a difference of kin or lineage, as in Vasily Tatishchev’s lexicon, where “inorodny distinguishes lineage”, even when two people share a faith and a ruler (his example is a baptized Tatar and a Russian: “co-religionists and countrymen, but by nature very different”). It became a legal category with the Statute on the Administration of Inorodtsy of 1822, written for the peoples of Siberia, and spread widely after the Code of Laws was published [“Inorodtsy”, 2014, 2014] confirmed. Pislegin finds that in the Vyatka region after the reforms, the gap between “inorodtsy” and Russians was “artificially strengthened” and that colorful prejudices spread: that non-Russians did not know the wheel, were all drunkards, and so on [Pislegin, 2023]. The Il’minsky system of the 1870s taught baptized non-Russians in their own languages, with Russian Orthodoxy as the goal [Tatarica, 2026] [Retish, 2002]. Retish’s summary is that Mari and Udmurts were seen as backward, and that scholars thought the best path was to adopt Russian culture and Orthodoxy [Retish, 2002].

Whether the Statute of 1822 itself applied to the Mari I did not check [unconfirmed]; the sources above show the term used broadly for non-Russian peoples by the 1860s.

6.4 The sorcerer image: how old, how common?

Today a Mari “sorcerer” is a familiar figure in Russian media. In 2008 the national newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda reported that sorcerers had helped solve a murder case in Mari El. In 2011 a hiker on a web forum asked, “Where can I find a real Mari sorcerer?”. A television series by the director Andrei Eshpai, who has Mari roots, shows a soothsayer helping Grand Prince Vasily III to father a son, the future Ivan IV; Luehrmann notes that nothing in the series says the man is Mari, but that the scene draws on the idea of the Mari as sorcerers [Luehrmann, 2013].

A Russian-language source from the field supports the point. A conference abstract by a student of ethnology at Moscow State University (Lomonosov conference, 2016), based on fieldwork in the Urzhum district of Kirov Oblast in 2015, says that “All Mari are sorcerers” is “a fairly stable concept” in ethnically mixed parts of the Volga region; that among non-Mari residents there is a wary attitude toward Mari ritual culture and their supposed great magical power; and that this stereotype is often negative, with Mari suspected of the “evil eye” and of casting spells. The same abstract reports that Mari respondents themselves took part readily in talk about witchcraft and saw magic as a feature of their own culture, though at first they answered that “Russians can also cast the evil eye” [Ustyantsev, 2016] confirmed. It is a short abstract from a small local study, so it shows that the idea exists, not how many people hold it [unconfirmed].

Luehrmann’s argument is that this reputation grew “from situations of close neighborly coexistence” between people of different faith, over several centuries, and that it does not go back to the conquest of 1552 [Luehrmann, 2013]. She points out that, in the mid-17th century, Russian villagers accused Mordvin neighbors of witchcraft in order to push them off land near Nizhny Novgorod. I found no period quotation of Russian peasants about Cheremis sorcery, so the early history of the folk image is thin in the sources I could read [unconfirmed].

6.5 The Multan affair, 1892–96

The Multan affair is about the Udmurts, a people related to the Mari, but it shows attitudes that shaped how Russians saw all the Volga Finno-Ugric peoples. Blood libel means the false charge that a minority group kills people in religious rituals; it was used against Jews in Europe for centuries.

Key dates
  1. May 1892A headless body of a Russian beggar is found near Staryi Multan
  2. Dec 1894Malmyzh: 7 of 10 Udmurt villagers convicted
  3. Sep–Oct 1895Elabuga retrial: again convicted
  4. 28 May–4 Jun 1896Mamadysh third trial: all acquitted

According to Vorontsov, an Udmurt historian who published the report on the case that the senior prosecutor Anatoly Koni sent to the justice minister, the investigation started on the discovery of the body of a Russian beggar, Konon Matyunin, on a path between two villages in May 1892; the investigation was led by a deputy prosecutor and, relying “on rumors and guesses”, tried “at all costs to prove the ritual nature of the crime”. It beat the accused, forged evidence and intimidated witnesses [Vorontsov, 2016] confirmed. Koni’s own report says the district police officer, “drawing from popular rumor that the Votyaks [Udmurts] perform a human sacrifice every forty years”, turned his attention to the neighboring half-Udmurt village of Staryi Multan [Vorontsov, 2016] confirmed.

Seven of ten accused were convicted in December 1894; the Senate overturned the verdict, and a second court at Elabuga convicted the seven again on 1 October 1895; the Senate overturned that one too. At the third trial, in Mamadysh on 28 May–4 June 1896, the defense, including the writer Vladimir Korolenko, showed the police acts to be unlawful and the medical and ethnographic “expert” conclusions groundless, and all were acquitted [Vorontsov, 2016] confirmed. Korolenko, who sat beside the accused in Elabuga, wrote of one convict, a church warden, whispering “Christ suffered…” when the verdict was read [Korolenko, 1895]. Koni recalled that the Senate’s second reversal “aroused considerable displeasure in St. Petersburg official circles”, and that the procurator of the Holy Synod, Konstantin Pobedonostsev, could not accept the Senate’s demand that any conviction for human sacrifice to pagan gods be reached with every legal formality observed [Vorontsov, 2016] confirmed.

Two sources differ on a detail: Vorontsov and Koni describe the victim as an adult Russian beggar, while Luehrmann says the peasants accused the Udmurts of killing “a child” [Vorontsov, 2016] [Luehrmann, 2013] disputed. I follow the primary document (Koni’s report), which describes an adult.

What it showed. Vorontsov argues that the “fabrication of ritual trials” in Nicholas I’s reign, fed by medieval legends, bred “rumors, prejudice and distrust” among Russians toward the inorodtsy; he names earlier cases of 1848–52 and 1854 in Malmyzh district and the Saratov case of 1853 against Jews and Germans [Vorontsov, 2016]. Luehrmann reads the Multan case as the Volga region’s equivalent of the European blood libel, and says land and village boundaries were again at stake; she adds that in her own fieldwork in Mari El in the 2000s she “still heard frequent warnings” to avoid Mari grove ceremonies because humans were sacrificed there [Luehrmann, 2013]. The last sentence is her report of what people said, and I could not check how widespread the warnings are [unconfirmed].

6.6 The Soviet decades

After 1917 the official language changed but the idea of backwardness remained, now in the form of “enlightenment”. Retish quotes a Soviet editorial of 1921 about the Udmurts: “after many centuries the star of enlightenment begins to shine… The morality and soul of the forgotten people is waking from a long nightmare”. He argues that under the tsarist, Provisional Government and Soviet regimes, non-Russians had “special cultural obligations” based on nationality [Retish, 2002]. The same Soviet state set up the Mari oblast, opened Mari schools (188 by 1920, by his count) and trained Mari staff [Retish, 2002]. It also accused national cadres of “bourgeois nationalism”, as in the Elchibaev case above [Oshaev, 2022].

In everyday life, Luehrmann records what an ethnic Russian woman in her forties, raised in a multi-ethnic railway settlement in Soviet-era Mari El, told her in 2005: that Mari women are “all witches” and that she should not accept food in a Mari village. The same woman asked her to note the address of any wise old woman she met, hoping a Mari healer could cure her “evil eye” [Luehrmann, 2013]. Luehrmann’s reading is that Mari magic is treated as “a fact of life”, and that such beliefs enfold the Mari rather than cast them out: Russian foresters avoid felling groves for fear of being cursed [Luehrmann, 2013]. That is one researcher’s observation from a few conversations, not a measured share of the population [unconfirmed].

6.7 Today

Surveys of Mari El. The Vasiliev Mari Research Institute surveyed 895 residents aged 15 and over in June 2001, in three towns, four urban-type settlements and six rural districts, using a quota sample. It asked people in each group whether they had met disrespect for their nationality [Regnum / Mari Research Institute, 12 Aug 2002]. The results, as reprinted by the Regnum agency in 2002, are in the chart below. Mari reported insult or disrespect more often than Russians or Tatars on each of the four items charted. On a broader item, meeting disrespect for one’s own nationality, the article gives 48.9% of Mari, 46.0% of Russians and 26.2% of Tatars, so Russians also report it; the article does not give the exact wording of that question. The headline says about 40% of Mari feel humiliated; the figures inside range from 25.7% to 48.9% depending on the item, so “40%” is a loose summary confirmed [unconfirmed].

The same survey asked a different question: which nationality do you feel greatest sympathy toward? Regnum’s text gives 53.3% of Russians naming Russians, 54.4% of Mari naming Mari, and only 1.5% of Russians naming Mari; 10.5% of Mari named Russians [Regnum / Mari Research Institute, 12 Aug 2002]. These are preferences for one’s own group and do not measure stereotypes.

A later study from the same institute is more optimistic. Vitaly Shabykov reports that in 1994, 2001 and 2006 about 82–84% of Russians and 76–82% of Mari said a person’s nationality does not matter to them in conversation, and that the share of Mari who want to talk only with their own people fell from 18.2% to 10.1% [Shabykov, 2015] confirmed. It also found that Mari were the group most likely to prefer a work team of their own nationality (27.9% in 2001, against about 17% of Russians and Tatars) [Shabykov, 2015]. So surveys show both good will and a sense of insult, and they do not measure the same thing.

National surveys. The Levada Center’s August 2018 poll, reported in the press, found a sharp rise in support for limiting residence of certain nationalities; the report names Roma (32%), Chinese (31%) and Vietnamese (26%) at the top. It does not mention the Mari [Levada Center, 27 Aug 2018] confirmed. I found no Levada or Russian Academy of Sciences (Institute of Ethnology and Anthropology) item on the Mari alone; the published national polls group nationalities in a way that leaves them out [unconfirmed].

Everyday speech and jokes. I found no collection or study of jokes about the Mari, and no representative survey on how many Mari hide or play down their identity in town [unconfirmed]. What I did find is the Mari side of the story.

How the Mari describe it. The singer Vyacheslav Sozonov, a soloist of the Mari opera and ballet theater, said in a 2020 interview: after the congress of 1918 the Mari decided “we ourselves do not call ourselves that”, “then it turned into a mockery (издевка), when we called ourselves Mari and people continued to call us Cheremis”. In his song “Cheremis” he proposes taking the old name back as a source of pride, linking it to the Cheremis wars. His collaborators said that many viewers wrote that they had thought the word insulting and now felt able to be proud [Realnoe Vremya / MariUver, 6 Nov 2020] confirmed. This is the view of one artist and his team; I did not find a poll of how Mari in general feel about the word [unconfirmed].

The Mari scholars Nina Glukhova and Vladimir Glukhov, summarizing the Mari researcher Sanukov (2002), write that Mari describe themselves with “perseverance and patience, industry and diligence”, as well as, among negatives, “shyness, diffidence, timidity”; they speak of “a national inferiority complex” [Glukhova & Glukhov, 2003]. That is a scholar’s interpretation of Mari self-description, and an unusual one to put in print; I could not read the original survey [unconfirmed].

Why it matters

A stereotype is an idea about a whole group repeated until it feels like common sense. The record here shows ideas changing with the needs of the day: fierce warriors when armies mattered, pagans when conversion mattered, backward peasants when empire and “enlightenment” mattered, and sorcerers in some modern media. It also shows that Mari today answer in their own words, as in the 1918 renaming and the 2020 song.

7. Language policy and the law of 2018

In the 1990s Mari El adopted laws that made Mari a state language together with Russian and provided for schools taught in Mari [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006] [Glukhova & Glukhov, 2003]. The Helsinki report says that roughly 21–22% of Mari El’s schoolchildren studied Mari in the early 2000s, and the numbers in the chart follow it [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006].

In 2018 Russia’s federal law no. 317-FZ of 3 August made learning a native language voluntary and dependent on a written application from parents, and Radio Svoboda reported on the worries of Mari teachers and parents in Mari El [Radio Svoboda, 2018] [Radio Svoboda, 2018] confirmed. The fall in the number of children learning Mari in Mari El was already clear before 2018, but the data I found do not cover 2005–2017, and I cannot measure how much of the later fall is due to the law [unconfirmed]. By 2018/19, 10.5% of pupils (7,775 of 74,085) studied Mari as a native language, according to Radio Svoboda; Fenno-Ugria reported in May 2024 about 8.6%, or 7,400 pupils [Radio Svoboda, 2018] [Fenno-Ugria, 30 May 2024]. These two figures may use different definitions, so they cannot be compared strictly disputed.

Why it matters

Language survives when children learn it at home and at school. A law that makes study voluntary shifts the decision to parents, who may face pressure to choose Russian for exams and jobs. Whether that explains the numbers is a question the data cannot settle.

8. Activists, Finno-Ugric ties, and a fact-check

The Mari national movement has mainly worked through cultural and civic groups: Mari Ushem, the All-Russia Congress of the Mari (convened every four years by its board, Mer Kanash) and a youth organization [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006]. Ties with Estonia, Finland and Hungary are real. In February 2005 a group of Finnish politicians and cultural figures appealed to Russian authorities to end the harassment of democratic opposition figures in Mari El and to find those who beat Kozlov [Kommersant, May 2005] confirmed. The Estonian foundation Fenno-Ugria describes itself as an umbrella body for cooperation with Estonians’ related peoples, founded in 1927 and refounded in 1991 [Fenno-Ugria, 2026] confirmed. It also reports on Mari rights; it is a cultural body and, in practice, an advocate, and its own reports are those of an interested party.

Recent pressure on those ties is documented by Fenno-Ugria and by Russian media. Russia’s Ministry of Justice listed the Estonian NGO Uralic Centre as “undesirable” on 30 August 2023. The Yoshkar-Ola court fined Mari Ushem (Mari Union) 50,000 rubles for a repost from that organization on 12 June 2024 [Fenno-Ugria, Dec 2024] confirmed, and Mediazona reported in September 2024 that a protocol on “undesirable organization” participation had been drawn up against Mari Ushem [Mediazona, 11 Sep 2024] confirmed. Fenno-Ugria says its own membership fell from 202 to 64 in early 2024 after Ministry of Justice action, and that library and school staff were harassed [Fenno-Ugria, Apr 2024] confirmed. Mediazona adds that in February 2020 a former Mari Ushem member in the pro-government All-Russia People’s Front, Vasily Petrov, founded a group with a similar name, “Mari ushem” (a different spelling), which collects aid for soldiers; Fenno-Ugria says the authorities created it [Mediazona, 11 Sep 2024] [Fenno-Ugria, Dec 2024] disputed.

Fact-check: “an armed Mari movement trained in Finnish camps”

ClaimWhat I foundVerdict
A Mari armed or terrorist movement exists.I found no source for armed groups. The only radical group in the record is Kugeze Mlande, which called for independence in 1990–95 and stayed a fringe movement [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006].unsupported
Mari are trained in camps in Finland.No source found. The nearest official statement, Surkov’s closed speech of 16 May 2005, says Finland, Estonia and the EU “have sharply stepped up” activity on Finno-Ugric peoples, that the regions where these are titular peoples hold “a strategic reserve of our oil”, and that it is “an obviously planned system of measures”. He does not mention weapons or camps in the text Kommersant quoted [Kommersant, May 2005].unsupported
Where the story came from.It began in a wave of articles in 2005, after the European Parliament resolution of 12 May: Rossiyskaya Gazeta wrote of “a project” for a “Greater Finno-Ugria” and of oil and mineral wealth; the weekly Zavtra compared Finno-Ugric autonomy with the North Caucasus. A Finnish commentator, Mika Parkkonen, read this as an effort to deflect criticism [Parkkonen, Oct 2005]. Jamestown noted that Putin replied to the criticism by speaking of a “very harmonious” coexistence of Slavic and Finno-Ugric tribes [Jamestown, 3 Aug 2005].confirmed
Separatism is not mainstream among Mari (as the starting text said).The main groups pursue language and culture; the pro-independence group was a fringe [IHF/MHG, Feb 2006].confirmed
Finno-Ugric ties are cultural only.Mostly cultural and humanitarian, but also political advocacy (appeals, press) [Kommersant, May 2005] [Fenno-Ugria, 2026].disputed
Why it matters

A claim becomes “true” in public debate by repetition. The test is simple: who said it first, in what words, and what evidence did they give? Here the trail leads to a political speech about oil and foreign pressure, not to any record of weapons.

Review questions, lesson 2

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

7Why is there no reliable percentage of Mari who follow the native religion?
Answer. The census asks no religion question, and the estimates that exist come from different sources (officials, surveys, scholars) that count different things. The “20–25%” in the starting text could not be matched to a measurement.
8What is dual faith, and what examples do the sources give?
Answer. People are baptized and attend church, but also take part in grove rites and see the Orthodox and Mari gods as one Creator. NG-Religii quotes clergy about sacrificial geese left under an icon of St. George.
9What did the European Parliament resolution of 12 May 2005 actually address, and what did it not say?
Answer. Human rights, press freedom, the 2004 election and equal language education. It does not name Markelov, and I found no use of the word “Russification”.
10Name one fringe separatist group and explain why it does not show that Mari separatism is mainstream.
Answer. Kugeze Mlande, which called for independence in 1990–95; it was a small splinter that broke from Mari Ushem and reportedly dissolved in 1995.
11Explain the term “inorodtsy” and say how historians use it to show attitudes toward the Mari.
Answer. A legal and everyday term in imperial Russia for non-Russian subjects (“people of another birth”). Pislegin and Retish show it linked to labels such as “wild”, “backward” and “filthy”, and to the policy of conversion and Russification through education.
12What did the Multan affair of 1892–96 show about attitudes toward the Volga Finno-Ugric peoples?
Answer. Rumors that pagans sacrificed people led to a false murder case against Udmurt villagers. The police acted on rumor, courts twice convicted, and only a third trial, after pressure from Korolenko, Koni and others, acquitted them. Vorontsov says such trials bred prejudice among Russians toward “inorodtsy”. The case concerned Udmurts, not Mari.
13A source says Mari people are “all witches”. How should a student treat that statement?
Answer. As a reported view, attributed to one person (a landlady interviewed by Luehrmann), not as a fact about the Mari. Luehrmann reads such views as part of a regional pattern in which Mari magic is feared and also sought out. Evidence on how common the belief is remains thin.
14What does the Mari Research Institute survey of 2001 show, and what can it not show?
Answer. Mari respondents reported being insulted in their national dignity more often than Russians or Tatars (for example 35.4% in the service sector against 21.5% and 27.7%). It does not say who offered the insult or how common stereotypes are, and the “40%” headline is loose.
15Why did Sozonov call the name “Cheremis” a mockery, and what does he propose?
Answer. After 1918 Mari called themselves Mari, but others still said “Cheremis”, which became an insult. He proposes reclaiming the name as a source of pride tied to the Cheremis wars of the 16th century.
16What can and cannot be said about the 2018 law and enrollment in Mari lessons?
Answer. Study became voluntary on parental application, and the documented share of pupils learning Mari fell (about 21% around 2004, 10.5% in 2018/19, 8.6% in 2024), but figures for 2005–2017 are missing and the measures differ, so the law’s causal effect is not established.
17What is the evidence for “an armed Mari movement trained in Finnish camps”?
Answer. None was found. The claim traces to a 2005 wave of press stories after Surkov’s speech about oil and foreign pressure; the Kommersant text of that speech mentions neither weapons nor camps.

Glossary

Archaeological culture
A set of sites sharing tools, pottery and building style, used to trace peoples before writing.
Blood libel
The false charge that a minority kills people in religious rites. Used against Jews in Europe, and in the Multan case against Udmurts.
Cheremis (cheremisy)
The Russian name for the Mari until the early 20th century. An exonym of uncertain origin.
Dual faith (dvoeverie)
Holding two religious traditions together, here Orthodox Christianity and the native religion.
Endangered language
A language whose number of users is falling so that it may stop being passed to children. Rated by bodies such as UNESCO; I did not check its rating of Mari.
Exonym
A name for a people given by outsiders (opposite: endonym or self-name).
Finno-Ugric
A branch of the Uralic family (everything but the Samoyedic languages). Many linguists doubt it is a true family unit.
Inorodtsy
Imperial Russian legal and everyday term for non-Russian subjects (“people of another birth”).
Isogloss
A feature (a sound change or a word) shared by some languages and not others, used to group them.
Kart
A priest of the Mari native religion.
Kugeze Mlande
“Ancestral Land”, a small group formed in late 1990 that called for independence of Mari El; fringe and reportedly dissolved in 1995.
Literary standard
An agreed written form of a language used in schools and print. Mari has two: Meadow-Eastern and Hill.
Mari Ushem
“Mari Union”, a national organization founded in 1917 and revived in 1990.
Permic
The branch of Uralic that includes Komi and Udmurt.
Protolanguage
The reconstructed common ancestor of a group of related languages.
Sacred grove
A stand of trees used for prayer and offerings in the Mari native religion.
Stereotype
A fixed, simplified idea about all members of a group.
Titular republic
A republic named after one nationality, here the Mari in Mari El.
Uralic
The language family that includes Finnish, Estonian, Hungarian, Saami, Komi, Udmurt, Mari, Mordvin and Samoyedic languages.
“Undesirable” organization
A Russian legal status that bans a foreign or international group’s activity and penalizes participation. Used in 2023 against the Estonian NGO Uralic Centre.

  • Maps: Natural Earth (public domain; admin-1 regions and rivers, naturalearthdata.com), projected with an Albers conic projection. The Uralic and Mari speaker areas come from Rantanen et al. (2022), Zenodo record 10555488, CC BY 4.0. No khanate borders are drawn because the sources disagree.
  • Charts and trees are drawn from the figures in the text. Where a bar rests on a secondary value it is marked.
